Something else which is interesting is that new pilots, simulator time or not, usually porpoise when first flying. I did not observe any of this. Porpoising occurs because the pilot constantly overcompensates to maintain level or a specific altitude. The result in that when above level they push down. When below level they pull up. The result is an cyclic up/down movement. Though perhaps did occur and just not in the video I've seen. edit: I have not checked the radar track.

Also worth pointing out that most non-pilots don't know that throttle setting adjusts altitude. To climb you increase throttle. To sink you pull it. Yet he didn't seem to have trouble sanely flying. Which leads us into trim adjustment. An aircraft this large is going to require a fair amount of force to properly control unless the control surfaces are properly trimmed. Simply burning fuel during flight requires trim adjustment. The aircraft was most certainly trimmed for it's previous landing OR neutrally trimmed. With low fuel this means it would almost certainly have a nose-up or nose-down attitude (depending on fuel load Cg -as Cg would have been shifted toward an extreme) and would require considerable forward or backward pressure to prevent crazy climbs or dives. Especially with full throttle during takeoff. It's very unlikely a non-pilot would even know to trim the aircraft or what the controls would look like. Especially if his only experience were "video games."

I bet I know the question. I've fielded that question many times. Everyone hates the answers. So allow me to take a guess.

The speed of jets at low altitude is frequently determined by two primary factors. One is control surface flutter. The second is impact safety. Neither of these limits physically prevent the aircraft from traveling well beyond its safe operating limits.

Sustained control surface flutter can damage the aircraft and fatigue metal. Taken to an extreme it can limit and even prevent control of the aircraft. Aluminum suffers from fatigue based catastrophic failure. So for the longevity of the skin it should be avoided. This doesn't mean it can't be done. Regardless, jets are commonly x-rayed to detect metal fatigue. Though I forget the exact mandatory schedule. It is ever couple of years or so. Though it may also be hour based.

The second issue is impact safety. The jets associated with 9/11+Twin Towers speed rating is based on the front windshield's ability to safely absorb a bird strike. Faster speeds are allowed as you increase altitude because fewer birds are higher. Most bird strikes are low to the ground and occur during takeoff or landing. The result is that you have a rating which exists strictly for pilot safety and is not reflective of airframe limitations. It's a window impact limitation.

There are also pragmatic operating windows to consider for some limits; which include fuel economy and engine longevity. Turbines are dramatically less expensive to operate at altitude and this creates cooler temps simply because the higher you go the cool it gets. This in turn increases fuel efficiency. When operating low the air is much denser which means you have to pump a lot more fuel to maintain combustion temp/mix. To improve cooling the engines tends to be run extra rich when low. Further decreasing fuel efficiency. Again, this tends to create pragmatic operating limits and not turbine or airframe limits.

TL;DR: Yes, the jets can in fact fly at the impact speeds. While possible control flutter was inducted it's unlikely it was enough to significantly negatively impact control of the aircraft.
